meta.title: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes and Alkenes (Cambridge International AS & A Level Chemistry)
meta.strand: Cambridge International AS & A Level Chemistry
meta.subject: Chemistry
meta.contentStandard: Cambridge International AS & A Level Chemistry 9701 (2025–2027 syllabus), Coursebook Chapter 15

learningOutcomes: Describe alkane structure, formulae, isomerism and naming.
Explain physical properties, combustion, pollution and radical substitution of alkanes.
Describe cracking and the bonding and reactions of alkenes, including the electrophilic addition mechanism.
Explain Markovnikov addition, oxidation by manganate(VII) and addition polymerisation.

sections.title: Alkanes: Structure and Naming
sections.goal: Describe alkane structure, formulae, isomerism and naming.

sections.title: Alkane Properties and Crude Oil
sections.goal: Explain boiling-point trends, low reactivity and fractional distillation.

sections.title: Combustion and Pollution
sections.goal: Write combustion equations and explain pollutants and catalytic converters.

sections.title: Free-Radical Substitution
sections.goal: Describe the radical chain mechanism of alkanes with halogens.

sections.title: Cracking
sections.goal: Explain cracking, compare thermal and catalytic methods, and complete cracking equations.

sections.title: Alkenes: Structure, Isomerism and Test
sections.goal: Describe the C=C bond, isomerism, reactivity and the bromine water test.

sections.title: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
sections.goal: Give reagents, conditions and products of alkene additions; compare atom economy and yield.

sections.title: Electrophilic Addition Mechanism
sections.goal: Draw the mechanism with curly arrows for HBr, Br2 and Cl2.

sections.title: Markovnikov Addition
sections.goal: Predict major products using carbocation stability.

sections.title: Oxidation of Alkenes
sections.goal: Predict products of cold and hot manganate(VII) oxidation and deduce alkenes.

sections.title: Addition Polymers and the Environment
sections.goal: Deduce repeat units and monomers; evaluate disposal and recycling.

sections.title: Exam Practice and Mastery
sections.goal: Apply calculations and deduction skills to exam-style tasks.

misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Only carbon and hydrogen; add other atoms and it is no longer a hydrocarbon.
Unsaturated means a C=C double or C≡C triple bond; C=O does not count.
Open-chain alkanes follow CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Saturated monocyclic hydrocarbons and open-chain hydrocarbons with exactly one C=C and no other multiple bonds follow CₙH₂ₙ.
Same molecular formula but different structures and properties.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: The longest chain must be drawn straight.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Bends in the drawing do not matter; count the longest continuous chain.
Only intermolecular forces are overcome.
Branching reduces surface contact and lowers it.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: CO is harmless because it is colourless.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: It binds to haemoglobin and is toxic.
Mostly from N₂ and O₂ in air at high temperature.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Radical substitution gives one pure product.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Further substitution and termination by-products such as ethane can form, so a mixture is expected.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: A fishhook arrow and a full curly arrow mean the same.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: A fishhook shows one electron; a full arrow shows a pair.
Cracking gives a shorter alkane and usually an alkene; check atom balance for each equation.
Simple alkenes are non-polar or weakly polar, but the π bond has exposed electron density.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Bromine water test: the result is "clear".
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: The correct observation is that orange bromine water becomes colourless. The word clear alone does not describe the colour change.
They show electron pair movement.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Br₂ cannot act as an electrophile because it is non-polar.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Approaching π electrons induce a dipole.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: HBr adds with equal amounts to both carbons.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: The more stable carbocation route is major.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Hot and cold KMnO4 give the same product.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Cold dilute gives a diol; hot concentrated cleaves.
The double bond is used up.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: A monomer has only two carbons.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Side groups such as phenyl and ethyl are allowed.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Addition polymers are all non-biodegradable and identical in hazard.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Most resist biodegradation, but burning PVC can release HCl, and dioxins may form under unsuitable conditions, unlike poly(ethene).

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Alkanes are unreactive only because they are non-polar.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Strong sigma bonds, low polarity, no functional group and high activation energies all contribute.
For but-2-ene they match, but E/Z depends on group priorities.
It can release HCl; dioxins may form under unsuitable combustion and cooling conditions.

misconceptionsAddressed.misconception: Percentage yield and atom economy are the same.
misconceptionsAddressed.howAddressed: Atom economy comes from the equation; yield from the experiment.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only. Crude oil is our main source of hydrocarbons, and it is also the starting point for most plastics. Look at the two molecules on screen. Ethane has only single bonds between its carbon atoms, so we call it saturated. Ethene has a carbon to carbon double bond, so we call it unsaturated. More generally, an unsaturated hydrocarbon contains carbon to carbon double or triple bonds. In this chapter we meet alkanes, which are saturated, and alkenes, which have one double bond. We will study their structures, names, properties and reactions step by step.
pauseCues: after 'A hydrocarbon is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only.'
narration.ttsText: A HY-droh-KAR-bun is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only. Crude oil is our main source of hydrocarbons, and it is also the starting point for most plastics. Look at the two molecules on screen. EE-thayn has only single bonds between its carbon atoms, so we call it saturated. EE-theen has a carbon to carbon double bond, so we call it unsaturated. More generally, an unsaturated HY-droh-KAR-bun contains carbon to carbon double or triple bonds. In this chapter we meet AL-kaynz, which are saturated, and AL-keenz, which have one double bond. We will study their structures, names, properties and reactions step by step.

keyIdeas: Alkenes: contain a C=C double bond

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Crude oil contains alkanes, cycloalkanes and arenes. Cycloalkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which there is a ring of three or more carbon atoms. Imagine joining the two terminal carbon atoms of a straight chain alkane to form a ring. Each terminal carbon originally has three hydrogen atoms. When the new carbon to carbon bond forms, each terminal carbon has two hydrogen atoms instead of three. The molecule therefore has two fewer hydrogen atoms overall. That is why cycloalkanes do not follow the alkane formula. Their general formula is C n H 2 n, but only for saturated hydrocarbons with one ring; molecules with more rings do not follow it. Cyclohexane, C 6 H 12, is drawn as a skeletal hexagon, and cyclopentane, C 5 H 10, as a pentagon. Every corner is a carbon atom. Notice that cyclobutane and but 1 ene both have the formula C 4 H 8, so a molecular formula alone cannot tell a ring from an alkene.
pauseCues: after 'Crude oil contains alkanes, cycloalkanes and arenes.'
narration.ttsText: Crude oil contains AL-kaynz, cycloalkanes and arenes. Cycloalkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which there is a ring of three or more carbon atoms. Imagine joining the two terminal carbon atoms of a straight chain AL-kayn to form a ring. Each terminal carbon originally has three hydrogen atoms. When the new carbon to carbon bond forms, each terminal carbon has two hydrogen atoms instead of three. The molecule therefore has two fewer hydrogen atoms overall. That is why cycloalkanes do not follow the AL-kayn formula. Their general formula is C n H 2 n, but only for saturated hydrocarbons with one ring; molecules with more rings do not follow it. Cyclohexane, C 6 H 12, is drawn as a skeletal hexagon, and cyclopentane, C 5 H 10, as a pentagon. Every corner is a carbon atom. Notice that cyclobutane and but 1 ene both have the formula C 4 H 8, so a molecular formula alone cannot tell a ring from an AL-keen.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: The alkanes form a homologous series, which is a family of compounds with the same general formula. For open chain alkanes the general formula is C n H 2 n plus 2. If a molecule has three carbon atoms, n equals three, and it has two times three plus two, which is eight hydrogen atoms. That gives propane. Look at the table: each step down adds one carbon and two hydrogen atoms, which is a CH 2 unit. Names end in a-n-e. Learn the first five names now. Notice that the formula applies to open chain alkanes only. Ring alkanes, called cycloalkanes, have a different formula, which we meet next.
pauseCues: after 'The alkanes form a homologous series, which is a family of compounds with the same general formula.'
narration.ttsText: The AL-kaynz form a hoh-MOL-uh-gus series, which is a family of compounds with the same general formula. For open chain AL-kaynz the general formula is C n H 2 n plus 2. If a molecule has three carbon atoms, n equals three, and it has two times three plus two, which is eight hydrogen atoms. That gives PROH-payn. Look at the table: each step down adds one carbon and two hydrogen atoms, which is a CH 2 unit. Names end in a-n-e. Learn the first five names now. Notice that the formula applies to open chain AL-kaynz only. Ring AL-kaynz, called cycloalkanes, have a different formula, which we meet next.

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Organic names are built from a stem that tells you how many carbon atoms are in the longest chain. Meth means one, eth means two, prop means three, but means four and pent means five. Then hex is six, hept is seven, oct is eight, non is nine and dec is ten. Notice that the first four, meth, eth, prop and but, are historical names you simply have to memorise. From pent onwards the stems come from Greek number words. Once you know the stem, you add an ending such as a-n-e or e-n-e to show the family.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: A homologous series has four features you must be able to state. First, all members share one general formula. Second, neighbouring members differ by one CH 2 unit. Third, they have the same functional group, so they react in similar ways. The functional group is the atom or group of atoms that decides how a molecule reacts. Fourth, the physical properties, such as boiling point, change gradually as the chain gets longer. In an exam, always link the similar chemistry to the shared functional group, and link the gradual change in physical properties to the increasing size of the molecule.

interactive.title: Comparative Molecular Geometry & Polarity Playground (CH₄, CO₂, NH₃, H₂O, PCl₅, SF₆)
interactive.instructions: Select molecules across steric numbers 2 to 6 to compare electron-domain geometry vs molecular shape, idealised vs measured bond angles, and 3D dipole polarity.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Comparative VSEPR molecular geometry playground for CH4, CO2, NH3, H2O, PCl5, and SF6
interactive.fallbackText: Compare CH4 (tetrahedral 109.5°, non-polar), CO2 (linear 180°, non-polar), NH3 (trigonal pyramidal ~107°, polar), H2O (bent 104.5°, polar), PCl5 (trigonal bipyramidal 90°/120°, non-polar), SF6 (octahedral 90°, non-polar).
interactive.modelNote: VSEPR predicts idealised electron-domain geometries; lone-pair–bonding-pair repulsion compresses measured angles (e.g. 109.5° → ~107° in NH₃ and 104.5° in H₂O).

examples.label: CH₄ (Tetrahedral)
examples.prompt: Methane (AX₄): 4 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs. Check geometry and overall polarity.
examples.successExplanation: CH₄ is symmetrically tetrahedral (109.5°) and overall non-polar.

examples.label: CO₂ (Linear)
examples.prompt: Carbon dioxide (AX₂): remember each C=O double bond counts as ONE electron domain!
examples.successExplanation: CO₂ is linear (180°); its two equal opposite C=O dipoles cancel, making CO₂ non-polar.

examples.label: NH₃ (Pyramidal)
examples.prompt: Ammonia (AX₃E): compare tetrahedral electron geometry with trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.
examples.successExplanation: NH₃ has tetrahedral electron geometry, trigonal pyramidal shape (~107°), and is polar.

examples.label: H₂O (Bent)
examples.prompt: Water (AX₂E₂): 2 bonding domains + 2 lone pairs compress the angle to ~104.5°.
examples.successExplanation: H₂O has tetrahedral electron geometry, bent shape (104.5°), and a strong net dipole (polar).

examples.label: PCl₅ (Expanded AX₅)
examples.prompt: A-Level expanded valence: Phosphorus pentachloride has 5 bonding domains around P.
examples.successExplanation: PCl₅ is trigonal bipyramidal (90° axial-equatorial / 120° equatorial) and symmetrical (non-polar).

examples.label: SF₆ (Expanded AX₆)
examples.prompt: A-Level expanded valence: Sulfur hexafluoride has 6 bonding domains around S.
examples.successExplanation: SF₆ is octahedral (90°) and completely symmetrical (non-polar).

hints: Count bonding domains (a double bond = 1 domain) + lone pairs to get electron-domain geometry.
Molecular shape ignores lone-pair positions but reflects their extra repulsion on bond angles.

narration.script: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. Pentane, C 5 H 12, has exactly three isomers, and you can see them as skeletal formulae. Pentane has a straight chain of five carbons. In 2-methylbutane the longest chain has four carbons with a methyl branch on the second carbon. In 2,2-dimethylpropane the longest chain has three carbons and two methyl branches on the middle carbon. Check that each drawing has five carbon atoms: count every corner and every line end. Chain isomers like these differ in the way the carbon skeleton is arranged. Different structures give different physical properties, such as boiling point.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Here are the naming rules. First, find the longest continuous carbon chain, which gives the parent name. Second, name the branches as alkyl groups, such as methyl and ethyl. Third, number the chain from the end that gives the lowest set of locants at the first point of difference. A locant is a number showing the position of a branch. On screen, numbering from the left puts the methyl on carbon two, but numbering from the right puts it on carbon four, so the left numbering is correct. Fourth, list the branches in alphabetical order and use di, tri or tetra for repeats. Di and tri are ignored when you alphabetise.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: There are two kinds of structural isomerism you need. Chain isomerism happens when the carbon skeleton is arranged differently. On screen, 2-methylpentane and 2,3-dimethylbutane both have the molecular formula C 6 H 14, but one has a methyl branch on carbon two of a five carbon chain, and the other has two methyl branches on a four carbon chain. Position isomerism happens when the carbon skeleton stays the same but a functional group is in a different position. But-1-ene and but-2-ene both have the formula C 4 H 8, and both have a four carbon chain, but the double bond is in a different place. In general, isomers have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms. Structural isomers have different structural formulae. Stereoisomers have the same structural formula but a different arrangement in space.

Position isomerism happens when the carbon skeleton stays the same but a functional group is in a different position. But-1-ene and but-2-ene both have the formula C 4 H 8, and both have a four carbon chain, but the double bond is in a different place. In general, EYE-suh-merz have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms. STRUK-chur-ul EYE-suh-merz have different STRUK-chur-ul formulae. Stereoisomers have the same STRUK-chur-ul formula but a different arrangement in space.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Alkane molecules are non polar. The only forces between them are instantaneous dipole induced dipole forces. Electrons move constantly, so for a moment one side of a molecule is slightly negative, which is a temporary dipole. That temporary dipole induces an opposite dipole in a neighbouring molecule, and the two attract. On screen you can see the boiling point graph rising from methane to pentane. A longer chain has more electrons and a larger surface area, so the attractions are stronger. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling point rises. When an alkane boils, no covalent bonds break.

narration.ttsText: AL-kayn molecules are non polar. The only forces between them are instantaneous dipole induced dipole forces. Electrons move constantly, so for a moment one side of a molecule is slightly negative, which is a temporary dipole. That temporary dipole induces an opposite dipole in a neighbouring molecule, and the two attract. On screen you can see the boiling point graph rising from MEE-thayn to PEN-tayn. A longer chain has more electrons and a larger surface area, so the attractions are stronger. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling point rises. When an AL-kayn boils, no covalent bonds break.

narration.script: Compare two isomers with the same molecular formula. Butane has a straight chain, so its molecules can lie side by side with a large area in contact. That gives stronger instantaneous dipole induced dipole forces. 2-methylpropane is branched and more compact, almost spherical, so its molecules touch over a smaller surface. The forces between them are weaker, and so less energy is needed to separate them. Therefore the branched isomer has the lower boiling point. When you answer in an exam, mention surface area of contact and the strength of the intermolecular forces, not just the word branching.

seedFaqs.q: Which has the higher boiling point, butane or 2-methylpropane?
seedFaqs.a: Butane, because it is straight-chain with more surface contact.

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: The coursebook explains that alkanes are generally unreactive. Several factors combine. The C to C and C to H sigma bonds are strong, so many reactions have high activation energies. Carbon and hydrogen differ very little in electronegativity. The carbon to hydrogen bonds are only weakly polar, so alkanes generally lack strongly electron deficient centres that attract nucleophiles. Alkanes also have no functional group and no exposed pi bond to attract electrophiles. In the test tube on screen, hexane, dyed purple, floats above water and the two layers do not mix, because non polar alkanes are immiscible with polar water. However, alkanes do react with oxygen in combustion, and with halogens in sunlight, as we shall see.

The carbon to hydrogen bonds are only weakly polar, so AL-kaynz generally lack strongly electron deficient centres that attract nucleophiles. AL-kaynz also have no functional group and no exposed PIE bond to attract electrophiles. In the test tube on screen, hexane, dyed purple, floats above water and the two layers do not mix, because non polar AL-kaynz are immiscible with polar water. However, AL-kaynz do react with oxygen in combustion, and with halogens in sunlight, as we shall see.

Low polarity; no functional group or π bond
High activation energies for many reactions

narration.script: At the refinery, crude oil is separated by fractional distillation in a tall column. The crude oil is heated, and the vapours rise up the column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top. Each fraction contains hydrocarbons with similar boiling points. Short chains condense near the top, as gases and gasoline, which gives us petrol. Naphtha is the starting material for many other chemicals. The longest chains, such as bitumen, stay at the bottom. Remember that every fraction is itself a mixture, and that this is a physical separation, not a chemical reaction.

stages.title: 1. Furnace & Bottom Residue (Bitumen, >350 °C)
stages.summary: Crude oil is heated to ~350 °C. Very long chains (>C₃₅) have strong London dispersion forces, never vaporise, and drain off as a viscous bitumen mixture.

prediction.prompt: Does each outlet pipe of a fractionating column produce one chemically pure alkane?
options: No — each fraction is still a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points
Yes — each pipe isolates one pure alkane isomer
prediction.explanation: Industrial fractional distillation separates crude oil into boiling-range mixtures (fractions), never single pure compounds.

stages.title: 2. Lower Column (Fuel Oil & Diesel, ~250–350 °C)
stages.summary: Long-chain vapours condense on lower bubble-cap trays where the temperature drops below their high boiling range.

stages.title: 3. Middle Column (Kerosene & Naphtha, ~100–250 °C)
stages.summary: Medium-chain hydrocarbon mixtures continue rising until they reach cooler middle trays and condense.

stages.title: 4. Top of Column (Petrol/Gasoline & Refinery Gas, <100 °C)
stages.summary: Short chains have weak London forces and low boiling points. Petrol condenses near the top; C₁–C₄ refinery gases exit uncondensed.

hints: Boiling point increases with chain length.
Hotter at the bottom, cooler at the top.

narration.script: When an alkane burns in a plentiful supply of oxygen, all the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen is oxidised to water. This is complete combustion, and it is strongly exothermic. The coursebook uses octane, one of the alkanes in petrol. Two octane molecules react with twenty five oxygen molecules to give sixteen carbon dioxide and eighteen water. The equation can also be written with a half, as one octane plus twelve and a half oxygen giving eight carbon dioxide and nine water. To balance, fix the carbon first, then the hydrogen, and finally the oxygen.

narration.script: Inside a car engine, the supply of oxygen is limited, so some of the fuel undergoes incomplete combustion and forms carbon monoxide instead of carbon dioxide. For octane, two molecules react with seventeen oxygen molecules to give sixteen carbon monoxide and eighteen water. Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas that bonds to the haemoglobin in your blood. The haemoglobin can then no longer carry oxygen around the body. Victims feel dizzy, then lose consciousness, and may die. Carbon monoxide is odourless, which is why faulty gas heaters in poorly ventilated rooms are so dangerous.

narration.script: Road traffic releases several pollutants. Carbon monoxide comes from incomplete combustion. In normal combustion, nitrogen in the air is not oxidised, but at the very high temperatures inside car engines, nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen oxides, mainly N O and N O 2. These reactions are reversible. Nitrogen oxides dissolve in rain to form acids and so contribute to acid rain, which kills trees, harms aquatic animals, erodes limestone and corrodes iron. Unburnt hydrocarbons, called volatile organic compounds, may be carcinogenic and contribute to photochemical smog, including P A N. Sulfur dioxide appears when fuels contain sulfur impurities.

narration.script: Look at the catalytic converter on screen. Precious metals such as platinum are coated on a honeycomb structure, which gives a large surface area for reactions. Once warm, it carries out three changes. Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide. Nitrogen oxides are reduced to harmless nitrogen. Unburnt hydrocarbons are oxidised to carbon dioxide and water. One equation is two C O plus two N O giving two C O 2 plus N 2. Some carbon monoxide is also oxidised by oxygen. Notice that the converter cannot reduce carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. In fact, removing carbon monoxide releases more carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming.

narration.script: Alkanes do not react with chlorine in the dark, but in ultraviolet light they undergo substitution, which means one atom is swapped for another. Methane and chlorine make chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. The mechanism involves free radicals. A free radical is an atom or group with an unpaired electron, and radicals are very reactive. The reaction is a chain reaction with three stages. Initiation makes radicals. Propagation uses a radical and makes another, so the chain keeps going. Termination removes radicals when two of them meet. We write a radical with a dot to show the unpaired electron.

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: In initiation, ultraviolet light supplies the energy to break the Cl to Cl bond by homolytic fission. In homolytic fission the bonding pair is shared equally, so each chlorine atom gets one electron, giving two chlorine radicals. In the first propagation step, a chlorine radical takes a hydrogen atom from methane, forming hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical. In the second propagation step, the methyl radical removes a chlorine atom from a chlorine molecule, forming chloromethane and a new chlorine radical. That new radical repeats step one, so the chain continues. Adding the two propagation steps gives the overall equation.

In the second propagation step, the methyl RAD-ih-kul removes a chlorine atom from a chlorine molecule, forming chloromethane and a new chlorine RAD-ih-kul. That new RAD-ih-kul repeats step one, so the chain continues. Adding the two propagation steps gives the overall equation.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: The overall reaction is methane plus bromine giving bromomethane and hydrogen bromide, in ultraviolet light. In initiation, the Br to Br bond breaks homolytically. Each fishhook arrow shows one electron moving, so two bromine radicals form, each with an unpaired electron shown as a dot. In propagation step one, a bromine radical removes a hydrogen atom from methane, forming hydrogen bromide and a methyl radical. In propagation step two, the methyl radical attacks a bromine molecule, forming bromomethane and a new bromine radical. That new radical can repeat step one, so the chain reaction continues. In each propagation step we start with a molecule and a radical, and finish with a different molecule and a different radical.
pauseCues: after 'The overall reaction is methane plus bromine giving bromomethane and hydrogen bromide, in ultraviolet light.'
narration.ttsText: The overall reaction is MEE-thayn plus bromine giving bromomethane and hydrogen bromide, in ultraviolet light. In initiation, the Br to Br bond breaks homolytically. Each fishhook arrow shows one electron moving, so two bromine radicals form, each with an unpaired electron shown as a dot. In propagation step one, a bromine RAD-ih-kul removes a hydrogen atom from MEE-thayn, forming hydrogen bromide and a methyl RAD-ih-kul. In propagation step two, the methyl RAD-ih-kul attacks a bromine molecule, forming bromomethane and a new bromine RAD-ih-kul. That new RAD-ih-kul can repeat step one, so the chain reaction continues. In each propagation step we start with a molecule and a RAD-ih-kul, and finish with a different molecule and a different RAD-ih-kul.

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Termination happens when two radicals meet and combine, which removes radicals from the reaction. Two chlorine radicals form chlorine, a chlorine radical and a methyl radical form chloromethane, and two methyl radicals form ethane. Notice that ethane is a by-product, and its presence is good evidence for this mechanism. The reaction does not stop at one substitution. Chloromethane can also be attacked by chlorine radicals to give dichloromethane, then trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane. So free radical substitution always gives a mixture of products. Using a large excess of methane makes mono substitution more likely.

narration.ttsText: Termination happens when two radicals meet and combine, which removes radicals from the reaction. Two chlorine radicals form chlorine, a chlorine RAD-ih-kul and a methyl RAD-ih-kul form chloromethane, and two methyl radicals form EE-thayn. Notice that EE-thayn is a by-product, and its presence is good evidence for this mechanism. The reaction does not stop at one substitution. Chloromethane can also be attacked by chlorine radicals to give dichloromethane, then trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane. So free RAD-ih-kul substitution always gives a mixture of products. Using a large excess of MEE-thayn makes mono substitution more likely.

narration.script: Termination steps are the final steps of the mechanism. Whenever two free radicals meet, they react with each other, and form a single non radical product. This removes those two radicals from the chain reaction, although other radicals in the mixture may still continue propagation. Look at the three examples on screen. Two bromine radicals combine to give a bromine molecule. A methyl radical and a bromine radical combine to give bromomethane. Two methyl radicals combine to give ethane. In each case two radicals go in and no radicals come out, which is the opposite of propagation, where a radical is regenerated. Notice each product molecule has all its electrons paired.

narration.ttsText: Termination steps are the final steps of the mechanism. Whenever two free radicals meet, they react with each other, and form a single non RAD-ih-kul product. This removes those two radicals from the chain reaction, although other radicals in the mixture may still continue propagation. Look at the three examples on screen. Two bromine radicals combine to give a bromine molecule. A methyl RAD-ih-kul and a bromine RAD-ih-kul combine to give bromomethane. Two methyl radicals combine to give EE-thayn. In each case two radicals go in and no radicals come out, which is the opposite of propagation, where a RAD-ih-kul is regenerated. Notice each product molecule has all its electrons paired.

keyIdeas: Those radicals leave the chain reaction

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Cracking is the process in which large, less useful hydrocarbon molecules are broken down into smaller, more useful molecules in an oil refinery. Lighter fractions, such as gasoline, are in high demand, and chemical engineers convert some of the excess heavier fractions into them. In the coursebook, large molecules are heated to a high temperature in a steel chamber with no oxygen, so combustion does not occur, and passed over an aluminium oxide catalyst. One example gives C 10 H 22 forming C 6 H 14 plus C 4 H 8. Cracking produces smaller alkanes and alkenes. The exact mixture depends on the feedstock, catalyst and conditions. The alkenes are very useful as the feedstock for plastics.

narration.script: The coursebook describes cracking with three features. There is no oxygen, so the hydrocarbons do not burn. The temperature is high. And an aluminium oxide catalyst is used. In industry, catalytic crackers often use zeolite catalysts at about four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, and thermal cracking uses higher temperatures and pressure without a catalyst. These numbers are representative operating conditions, not fixed values. The products are smaller alkanes, used as fuels, and alkenes, used for chemicals and polymers. Their proportions depend on the feedstock, the catalyst and the conditions, so be careful not to say that one fixed set of products always forms.

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: To complete a cracking equation, conserve atoms. Count the carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms in the large molecule, subtract those in the known product, and what is left is the missing product. In the first example, twelve carbons minus eight leaves four, and twenty six hydrogens minus eighteen leaves eight, so the missing product is C 4 H 8, an alkene. In the second, nine carbons minus seven leaves two, and twenty hydrogens minus sixteen leaves four, so the missing product is C 2 H 4, ethene. In the third, the leftover is four carbons and eight hydrogens, which can be two molecules of C 2 H 4. Finally, check that all carbon and hydrogen atoms are conserved and that your products are consistent with those given in the question.

narration.script: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons. An open chain alkene with one double bond has the general formula C n H 2 n, and ethene, C 2 H 4, is the first member. The double bond has two parts. The sigma bond is formed by head on overlap of orbitals along the line between the nuclei, as in the left diagram. The pi bond is formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals, as in the right diagram, and it puts electron density above and below the plane of the molecule. Each carbon in the double bond has three bonding regions, so the atoms around it are planar with bond angles of about 120 degrees. Rotation about the double bond is restricted.

narration.script: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the pi bond. The four electrons in the double bond create an area of high electron density, which attracts electrophiles. An electrophile is a species that accepts a pair of electrons. Simple hydrocarbon alkenes are non polar or only weakly polar overall, but the exposed pi electrons still make them open to attack. When an alkene reacts, one bond of the double bond breaks, and a new single bond forms to each carbon, which is called addition. To name an alkene, the parent chain must contain the double bond. Number from the end that gives the double bond the lowest number, as in but 1 ene and but 2 ene.

narration.ttsText: AL-keenz are more reactive than AL-kaynz because of the PIE bond. The four electrons in the double bond create an area of high electron density, which attracts electrophiles. An ih-LEK-troh-fyl is a species that accepts a pair of electrons. Simple HY-droh-KAR-bun AL-keenz are non polar or only weakly polar overall, but the exposed PIE electrons still make them open to attack. When an AL-keen reacts, one bond of the double bond breaks, and a new single bond forms to each carbon, which is called addition. To name an AL-keen, the parent chain must contain the double bond. narration.script: To test whether a compound is unsaturated, shake it with bromine water. Bromine water is orange or yellow, depending on its concentration. Look at the three test tubes. On the left is the bromine water. In the middle, an alkene has been added and shaken, and the mixture is colourless. On the right an alkane has been added, and the mixture stays orange. In the examination, state the colour change fully: orange to colourless. Do not say clear. The simple equation is that bromine adds across the double bond to give a dibromoalkane. In aqueous solution, other products can form too, but you need only the dibromo product for this course.

narration.script: Alkenes show two kinds of isomerism. Position isomers, such as but 1 ene and but 2 ene, have the double bond in a different place. Alkenes can also show cis and trans isomerism. In cis but 2 ene, the two methyl groups are on the same side of the double bond. In trans but 2 ene, they are on opposite sides. The more general E and Z system uses the priorities of the groups on each carbon: Z means the higher priority groups are on the same side, and E means opposite sides. For but 2 ene, cis is Z and trans is E. This happens because the pi bond stops rotation about the double bond, so one isomer cannot turn into the other at room temperature. Each carbon of the double bond must have two different groups.

narration.ttsText: AL-keenz show two kinds of isomerism. Position EYE-suh-merz, such as but 1 ene and but 2 ene, have the double bond in a different place. AL-keenz can also show cis and trans isomerism. In cis but 2 ene, the two methyl groups are on the same side of the double bond. In trans but 2 ene, they are on opposite sides. The more general E and Z system uses the priorities of the groups on each carbon: Z means the higher priority groups are on the same side, and E means opposite sides. For but 2 ene, cis is Z and trans is E. This happens because the PIE bond stops rotation about the double bond, so one isomer cannot turn into the other at room temperature. Each carbon of the double bond must have two different groups.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: In an addition reaction, one of the two bonds in the carbon to carbon double bond breaks, and a new single bond forms from each of the two carbon atoms. The general reaction is the alkene plus X Y giving a saturated product with X on one carbon and Y on the other. With hydrogen over a finely divided platinum or nickel catalyst, with heat, an alkane forms. With a concentrated hydrogen halide solution at room temperature, a halogenoalkane forms. With steam, using concentrated phosphoric acid as catalyst at high temperature and pressure, an alcohol forms. With chlorine or bromine solution at room temperature, a dihalogenoalkane forms. Learn every reagent, condition and product.

narration.ttsText: In an addition reaction, one of the two bonds in the carbon to carbon double bond breaks, and a new single bond forms from each of the two carbon atoms. The general reaction is the AL-keen plus X Y giving a saturated product with X on one carbon and Y on the other. With hydrogen over a finely divided platinum or nickel catalyst, with heat, an AL-kayn forms. With a concentrated hydrogen halide solution at room temperature, a HAL-oh-jen-oh-AL-kayn forms. With steam, using concentrated phosphoric acid as catalyst at high temperature and pressure, an alcohol forms. With chlorine or bromine solution at room temperature, a dihalogenoalkane forms. Learn every reagent, condition and product.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Hydrogenation is the addition reaction of alkenes with hydrogen. When ethene and hydrogen gas are heated and passed over a finely divided platinum or nickel catalyst, ethane forms. On screen, the new carbon hydrogen bonds are in red. The pi bond has gone, but the carbon to carbon sigma bond remains. This reaction is used in margarine manufacture. Unsaturated oils, such as sunflower oil, have hydrocarbon chains with several double bonds. They are partially hydrogenated, which straightens the chains, raises the melting point, and changes the liquid into a soft solid that spreads easily. Not every double bond reacts, so the product is partially saturated.

narration.ttsText: Hydrogenation is the addition reaction of AL-keenz with hydrogen. When EE-theen and hydrogen gas are heated and passed over a finely divided platinum or nickel catalyst, EE-thayn forms. On screen, the new carbon hydrogen bonds are in red. The PIE bond has gone, but the carbon to carbon SIG-muh bond remains. This reaction is used in margarine manufacture. Unsaturated oils, such as sunflower oil, have HY-droh-KAR-bun chains with several double bonds. They are partially hydrogenated, which straightens the chains, raises the melting point, and changes the liquid into a soft solid that spreads easily. Not every double bond reacts, so the product is partially saturated.

narration.script: Look at the two addition reactions on screen. When ethene meets hydrogen bromide at room temperature, bromoethane forms. A hydrogen atom adds to one carbon and a bromine atom to the other, shown in red. When ethene reacts with bromine, 1,2-dibromoethane forms, with one bromine atom on each carbon of the former double bond. This is the reaction behind the bromine water test, and chlorine behaves in the same way. In both cases the product has only single bonds, so it is saturated. Notice that the molecular drawings are balanced: each carbon still has four bonds. Check valency every time you draw a product.

narration.script: In industry, alkenes react with steam to make alcohols. Ethene and steam react at a high temperature and pressure in the presence of concentrated phosphoric acid as a catalyst, giving ethanol. On screen we use a reversible arrow, because ethanol can break down to ethene and water again. Representative industrial conditions are about three hundred degrees Celsius and sixty to seventy atmospheres. The coursebook says only high temperature and pressure, so treat those numbers as supplementary industrial detail. The hydroxyl group adds to one carbon and the hydrogen to the other, shown in red. The ethanol in alcoholic drinks is made differently, by fermentation of glucose.

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Atom economy and percentage yield are different ideas. Atom economy tells you how much of the total mass of the products is the useful product, as a percentage. It is calculated from the equation, before any experiment. Percentage yield tells you how much product you actually made compared with the theoretical maximum. Addition reactions, where the reactants simply join, have one hundred percent atom economy, such as ethene plus steam making ethanol. Substitution has lower atom economy, because a second product forms. For methane and chlorine making chloromethane and hydrogen chloride, the useful product is fifty point five out of eighty seven point zero, which is fifty eight point zero percent.

narration.script: Before the mechanism, we compare two ways to break a covalent bond. In homolytic fission, each atom takes one electron from the bonding pair, so two radicals form. We draw this with single headed arrows, called fishhook arrows, one for each electron. In heterolytic fission, one atom takes both electrons, so a positive and a negative ion form. We draw this with one full headed curly arrow, which shows the movement of an electron pair. A curly arrow starts at the bond or lone pair that the electrons come from, and finishes where they end up. An electrophile is a species that accepts a pair of electrons.

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: HBr is a polar molecule, because bromine is more electronegative than hydrogen. The hydrogen carries a partial positive charge and the bromine carries a partial negative charge. In the mechanism, the hydrogen atom acts as the electrophile, accepting a pair of electrons from the carbon to carbon double bond. Follow the first curly arrow on screen. It starts at the double bond and finishes at the hydrogen atom, so the pair of electrons forms a new carbon to hydrogen bond. The second curly arrow starts at the H to Br bond and finishes on the bromine atom. This is heterolytic fission, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion.

interactive.title: Electrophilic Addition of HBr to Ethene (6-Stage Mechanism)
interactive.instructions: Step carefully through electron-pair movement, heterolytic cleavage, carbocation intermediate formation, and nucleophilic attack by Br⁻. Total atoms (C₂H₅Br) and net charge (0) are conserved at every stage.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Six-stage electrophilic addition mechanism of HBr to ethene
interactive.fallbackText: 1. Polar Hδ+–Brδ- approaches C=C. 2. π-bond electron pair attacks Hδ+. 3. H–Br breaks heterolytically. 4. CH3CH2+ carbocation + :Br- intermediate. 5. :Br- lone pair attacks C+. 6. Bromoethane CH3CH2Br.

stages.title: 1. Reactants & Bond Polarity
stages.summary: Bromine is more electronegative than hydrogen, creating a permanent dipole Hδ⁺–Brδ⁻ near the electron-rich C=C π bond.

stages.title: 2. π-Bond Electron-Pair Movement
stages.summary: A full-headed curly arrow starts from the C=C π bond and points to the electrophilic Hδ⁺ atom.
stages.whatChanges: The exposed π electron cloud donates an electron pair to Hδ⁺.

reactionMeta.electronMovement: Full-headed arrow from C=C π bond to Hδ⁺

stages.title: 3. Heterolytic Cleavage of H–Br
stages.summary: Simultaneously, the H–Br bonding electron pair moves entirely onto Br (heterolytic fission).

stages.title: 4. Carbocation & Bromide Intermediate
stages.summary: A positively charged ethyl carbocation (CH₃–CH₂⁺) and a negatively charged bromide ion (:Br⁻) form; overall charge remains 0.

stages.title: 5. Bromide Lone-Pair Donation
stages.summary: A full-headed curly arrow starts from a lone pair on :Br⁻ and points directly to the positively charged carbon atom.

stages.title: 6. Bromoethane Product
stages.summary: A new C–Br σ bond forms, giving neutral bromoethane (CH₃CH₂Br) with all carbons tetravalent.

sequenceChallenge.explanation: First polar HBr approaches C=C, then the π-bond pair attacks Hδ⁺ to form the carbocation + Br⁻ intermediate, and finally Br⁻ donates a lone pair to give bromoethane.

narration.script: In step two, the bromide ion has a lone pair of electrons and is attracted to the positively charged carbon. On screen, the curly arrow starts at the lone pair and finishes at the positive carbon, where the new carbon to bromine bond forms. The product is bromoethane. narration.script: How can a non polar molecule like bromine act as an electrophile? As the bromine molecule approaches ethene, the area of high electron density around the double bond repels the pair of electrons in the Br to Br bond away from the nearer bromine atom. This makes the nearer bromine slightly positive and the further bromine slightly negative. This is an induced dipole. In the first curly arrow on screen, the pair of electrons moves from the double bond to the delta plus bromine. In the second curly arrow, the Br to Br bond breaks heterolytically and its electron pair moves onto the further bromine. That forms a carbocation and a bromide ion.

narration.ttsText: How can a non polar molecule like bromine act as an ih-LEK-troh-fyl? As the bromine molecule approaches EE-theen, the area of high electron density around the double bond repels the pair of electrons in the Br to Br bond away from the nearer bromine atom. This makes the nearer bromine slightly positive and the further bromine slightly negative. This is an induced dipole. In the first curly arrow on screen, the pair of electrons moves from the double bond to the delta plus bromine. In the second curly arrow, the Br to Br bond breaks heterolytically and its electron pair moves onto the further bromine. That forms a KAR-boh-KAT-eye-un and a bromide ion.

narration.script: Chlorine reacts with ethene by the same simplified electrophilic addition pattern as bromine, as the coursebook presents it. More detailed mechanisms exist, such as the bromonium ion model on the next slide, which is enrichment. The syllabus asks you to describe electrophilic addition, using bromine and ethene as an example, and the coursebook uses this simplified two step version. In the top row, the approaching ethene induces a dipole in the chlorine molecule. The electron pair from the double bond moves to the delta plus chlorine, and the Cl to Cl bond breaks heterolytically, giving a carbocation and a chloride ion. In the bottom row, the lone pair on the chloride ion attacks the positive carbon. The product is 1,2-dichloroethane. Chlorine acts as an electrophile because it accepts a pair of electrons. The coursebook asks you to explain how a chlorine molecule can act as an electrophile, so practise explaining the induced dipole in words as well as drawing it.

narration.script: This slide is enrichment. The coursebook draws the simplified mechanism, so practise that first, and ask your teacher how your examination answers should be framed. Chemists have found that the reaction of bromine with an alkene is better described by a cyclic bromonium ion, a three membered ring in which the bromine bears a positive charge. The bromide ion then attacks from the opposite side of the ring. That model explains the stereochemistry seen in real reactions. A second advanced point concerns bromine water. Because water is present in large amounts, it can also attack the intermediate, and so a compound called a bromohydrin, with a bromine on one carbon and an O H on the other, can form alongside the dibromo product. The bromine water test observation does not change: orange to colourless.

narration.ttsText: This slide is enrichment. The coursebook draws the simplified mechanism, so practise that first, and ask your teacher how your examination answers should be framed. Chemists have found that the reaction of bromine with an AL-keen is better described by a cyclic broh-MOH-nee-um ion, a three membered ring in which the bromine bears a positive charge. The bromide ion then attacks from the opposite side of the ring. That model explains the stereochemistry seen in real reactions. A second advanced point concerns bromine water. narration.script: Propene is unsymmetrical, so with longer asymmetric alkenes there are always two possible products. On screen, if the hydrogen adds to the end carbon, the positive charge sits on the middle carbon, giving a secondary carbocation and then 2-bromopropane. If the hydrogen adds to the middle carbon, the positive charge is on the end carbon, giving a primary carbocation and then 1-bromopropane. The coursebook states that where two addition products are possible, the major product is the one with the halogen atom bonded to the carbon of the double bond with the highest number of alkyl groups. Here that is 2-bromopropane. The primary route gives only a minor product.

narration.script: Carbocations are named by the number of alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon. A primary carbocation has one, a secondary has two and a tertiary has three. Each alkyl group tends to donate electrons along its bond to the positively charged carbon. This is the positive inductive effect, written plus I. It makes the positive charge less concentrated, which stabilises the ion. So a tertiary carbocation is the most stable and a primary carbocation is the least stable. A more stable intermediate forms more readily, so the product that comes from it is the major product. In the exam, say alkyl groups donate electrons, spreading the charge.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: The coursebook teaches that alkenes can be oxidised by acidified potassium manganate seven, a powerful oxidising agent. If an alkene is shaken with a cold, dilute acidified solution, the pale purple solution turns colourless, and the alkene is converted into a diol, a compound with two alcohol O H groups. On screen, ethene becomes ethane 1,2 diol, with one O H group on each carbon of the former double bond. Propene becomes propane 1,2 diol. The carbon chain stays intact. The equation uses O in square brackets to show oxygen from the oxidising agent. For propene: C H 3 C H double bond C H 2 plus water plus O gives C H 3 C H O H C H 2 O H.

narration.ttsText: The coursebook teaches that AL-keenz can be oxidised by acidified potassium MANG-uh-nayt seven, a powerful oxidising agent. If an AL-keen is shaken with a cold, dilute acidified solution, the pale purple solution turns colourless, and the AL-keen is converted into a DY-ol, a compound with two alcohol O H groups. On screen, EE-theen becomes EE-thayn 1,2 DY-ol, with one O H group on each carbon of the former double bond. PROH-peen becomes PROH-payn 1,2 DY-ol. The carbon chain stays intact. The equation uses O in square brackets to show oxygen from the oxidising agent. For PROH-peen: C H 3 C H double bond C H 2 plus water plus O gives C H 3 C H O H C H 2 O H.

keyIdeas: Product: a diol with two OH groups

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Now apply the same idea to but 2 ene. When shaken with cold, dilute, acidified potassium manganate seven, each carbon of the double bond gains one O H group, so the product is butane 2,3 diol. The purple solution becomes colourless. The four carbon chain is intact, and the two O H groups are on carbons two and three. The equation is C H 3 C H double bond C H C H 3 plus water plus O giving C H 3 C H O H C H O H C H 3. Name the diol by finding the longest chain, numbering to give the lowest locants to the O H groups, and using the ending d i o l. As always, this practical is a teacher demonstration only.

narration.script: Under harsh conditions, with hot, concentrated acidified potassium manganate seven, the carbon to carbon double bond is broken completely. Look at each carbon of the double bond separately. A carbon with two hydrogen atoms is oxidised to carbon dioxide. A carbon with one hydrogen and one alkyl group is first oxidised to an aldehyde, which is then further oxidised to a carboxylic acid. A carbon with two alkyl groups is oxidised to a ketone. The alkyl groups are labelled R. The two products show the position of the double bond in the original alkene, which is why this reaction is useful to chemists for working out structures.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Now we apply the rules to three alkenes. Cut each double bond at the dotted line and oxidise each carbon separately. In propene, the C H 2 carbon gives carbon dioxide and water, and the C H C H 3 carbon gives ethanoic acid, so the equation uses five O. In 2-methylpropene, the C H 2 carbon gives carbon dioxide and water, and the carbon with two methyl groups gives propanone, a ketone, using four O. In 2-methylbut-2-ene, one carbon has two methyl groups and gives propanone. The other has one hydrogen and a methyl group, and gives ethanoic acid, using three O. In each case the number of carbon atoms in the products equals the number in the alkene.

narration.ttsText: Now we apply the rules to three AL-keenz. Cut each double bond at the dotted line and oxidise each carbon separately. In PROH-peen, the C H 2 carbon gives carbon dioxide and water, and the C H C H 3 carbon gives eth-uh-NOH-ik acid, so the equation uses five O. In 2-methylpropene, the C H 2 carbon gives carbon dioxide and water, and the carbon with two methyl groups gives PROH-puh-nohn, a KEE-tohn, using four O. In 2-methylbut-2-ene, one carbon has two methyl groups and gives PROH-puh-nohn. The other has one hydrogen and a methyl group, and gives eth-uh-NOH-ik acid, using three O. In each case the number of carbon atoms in the products equals the number in the AL-keen.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: To identify the original alkene, work backwards from the oxidation products. First, name the two products. A carboxylic acid came from a carbon with one hydrogen and one alkyl group. A ketone came from a carbon with two alkyl groups. Carbon dioxide came from a carbon with two hydrogens, so if carbon dioxide is given off, the double bond was between the end two carbon atoms of the alkene. Remove the oxygen, join the two carbon atoms with a double bond, and add the hydrogen atoms and groups back. Finally, count the carbon atoms: they must equal the total in the two products. Propanone and ethanoic acid give 2-methylbut-2-ene.

narration.ttsText: To identify the original AL-keen, work backwards from the oxidation products. First, name the two products. A carboxylic acid came from a carbon with one hydrogen and one alkyl group. A KEE-tohn came from a carbon with two alkyl groups. Carbon dioxide came from a carbon with two hydrogens, so if carbon dioxide is given off, the double bond was between the end two carbon atoms of the AL-keen. Remove the oxygen, join the two carbon atoms with a double bond, and add the hydrogen atoms and groups back. Finally, count the carbon atoms: they must equal the total in the two products. PROH-puh-nohn and eth-uh-NOH-ik acid give 2-methylbut-2-ene.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Here are five reverse deductions, in increasing difficulty. In the first, carbon dioxide means an end carbon with two hydrogens, and ethanoic acid means a carbon with one hydrogen and a methyl group, so the alkene is propene. In the second, propanone and carbon dioxide give 2-methylpropene. In the third, two carboxylic acids with three carbons and two carbons give pent 2 ene, where the double bond is between carbons two and three. In the fourth, butanone and carbon dioxide give 2-methylbut-1-ene. In the fifth, only one product, propanone, forms from both ends, so the alkene is symmetrical: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene. For an alkene that exhibits E Z isomerism, oxidative cleavage generally cannot distinguish the two stereoisomers, because both produce the same fragments. Try covering the right column and deducing each alkene first, on paper.

In the fourth, butanone and carbon dioxide give 2-methylbut-1-ene. In the fifth, only one product, PROH-puh-nohn, forms from both ends, so the AL-keen is symmetrical: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Addition polymerisation is the reaction of many monomers containing at least one carbon to carbon double bond to form long chain polymers as the only product. On screen, many ethene molecules join. The pi bond in each C double bond C breaks, and then the monomers link together. The section in the square brackets is the repeat unit, with continuation bonds going through the brackets and a subscript n showing that the unit repeats, up to ten thousand times for poly ethene. The two carbon atoms of each double bond become the backbone of the chain. Because the polymer is the only product, no small molecule is lost.

narration.script: In poly alkenes made from one type of monomer, the repeat unit is the same as the monomer except that the carbon to carbon double bond is changed into a single bond. On screen, propene has a methyl side group, so poly propene has methyl groups sticking out of the carbon skeleton. Chloroethene, once called vinyl chloride, gives poly chloroethene, known as P V C. Tetrafluoroethene gives P T F E, used in non stick pans. In each case the side groups stay attached, and the continuation bonds go through the square brackets. Draw the repeat unit with correct brackets, continuation bonds and the subscript n.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Now two monomers with bigger side groups. Phenylethene, also called styrene, has a benzene ring attached to one carbon of the double bond. The polymer is poly phenylethene, with a phenyl group on every other backbone carbon. But 1 ene has an ethyl group on the double bond carbon, so the repeat unit has a C 2 H 5 side group. In both cases, the double bond opens, the two carbon atoms of the double bond stay in the backbone, and the large groups hang off as side groups. This shows that a monomer can contain many more than two carbon atoms: phenylethene has eight, and but 1 ene has four. Show the brackets, the continuation bonds and the subscript n.

This shows that a monomer can contain many more than two carbon atoms: FEE-nyl-EE-theen has eight, and but 1 ene has four. Show the brackets, the continuation bonds and the subscript n.

Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: A monomer used in addition polymerisation can contain more than two carbon atoms. The two carbon atoms that originally formed the double bond become the backbone of the polymer, and any other groups remain as side groups. To find the monomer, first split the polymer chain into repeat units. Here the repeating pattern is two backbone carbons, one with a phenyl ring and one with only hydrogens. Then put the C double bond C back into the monomer. The monomer is phenylethene, which has eight carbon atoms in total. Always check that each carbon in your monomer has four bonds.

narration.script: Here is a polymer section with ethyl groups on alternate carbon atoms. First split the chain into repeat units. The pattern repeats every two backbone carbons: one with an ethyl group and one with hydrogens only. Draw one repeat unit inside brackets, then change the two backbone carbons from a single bond back to a double bond. The monomer is C H 2 double bond C H C 2 H 5, which is but 1 ene. Check that each carbon has four bonds. The coursebook also asks: if a waste batch of this polymer were burned in an inefficient industrial incinerator, which toxic gas could be released? The answer is carbon monoxide, from incomplete combustion.

narration.script: Plastics are widely used, but large scale use has created a disposal problem. Poly alkenes are effectively huge alkane molecules, so they resist chemical attack and can take hundreds of years to decompose in landfill. The coursebook describes them as non biodegradable, so waste poly alkenes pollute the environment for centuries, as plastic sachets and carrier bags do when they block drains in Ghanaian towns. The table compares options. Reuse reduces waste. Recycling by melting and re moulding saves raw materials but needs careful sorting by recycling code. Chemical or feedstock recycling breaks polymers into useful chemicals but needs energy. Landfill is simple but leaves persistent waste.

narration.script: One way to deal with waste poly alkenes is to burn them and use the energy to generate electricity. If hydrocarbons burn in excess oxygen, the products are carbon dioxide and water. Incineration releases carbon dioxide and is not a zero carbon process. Its overall greenhouse gas impact depends on the waste being burned, the energy recovered and the alternative disposal method. Incomplete combustion produces toxic carbon monoxide. Burning poly chloroethene can release acidic hydrogen chloride gas, and under unsuitable combustion and cooling conditions, toxic chlorinated compounds, including dioxins, may also form. Controlled industrial incinerators use very high temperatures and gas cleaning. These are facts for evaluation only: students must never burn plastics, because the fumes are dangerous.

narration.script: The balanced equation is C 3 H 8 plus 5 O 2 giving 3 C O 2 plus 4 H 2 O. The ratio of propane to oxygen to carbon dioxide is one to five to three. A typical marking approach gives one mark for the correct equation, one for the ratio, and one for each correct volume with units. narration.script: Propanone has three carbons, so it came from a carbon with two methyl groups, written equals C open bracket C H 3 close bracket 2. Ethanoic acid has two carbons, so it came from a carbon with one hydrogen and a methyl group, written equals C H C H 3. Joining these two carbons by a double bond gives C H 3, twice, attached to the first carbon, double bond, then C H C H 3. That is C H 3 twice, C, double bond, C H, C H 3. The longest chain containing the double bond has four carbons with a methyl branch on carbon two, so the name is 2 methylbut 2 ene. Check: five carbons, ten hydrogens. narration.script: The relative formula mass of ethene is twenty eight point zero. For 1,2-dibromoethane, two carbons give twenty four, four hydrogens give four, and two bromines give one hundred and sixty, a total of one hundred and eighty eight point zero. Part a: moles of ethene are five point six zero divided by twenty eight point zero, which is zero point two zero zero. Part b: the ratio is one to one, so the theoretical mass is zero point two zero zero times one hundred and eighty eight, which is thirty seven point six grams. The percentage yield is thirty three point eight four divided by thirty seven point six, times one hundred, which is ninety point zero percent. Part c: seventy five percent of thirty seven point six grams is twenty eight point two grams. Practice guidance, not an official mark scheme.

narration.ttsStyleInstruction: Speak warmly and clearly, like a patient British chemistry teacher explaining to AS and A Level students. Steady pace with short natural pauses, slower for mechanisms. Say formulae in words: 'C n H 2 n plus 2'; 'delta plus' and 'delta minus' for partial charges; 'Br dot' for a radical; 'plus' and 'minus' for ion charges; 'potassium manganate seven' for KMnO4; 'sigma' and 'pi' for bonds; 'one comma two dibromoethane' for 1,2-dibromoethane.
narration.script: Let us recap the chapter. Open chain alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula C n H 2 n plus 2. They are fairly unreactive because their sigma bonds are strong and of low polarity, they have no functional group, and many reactions have high activation energies, but they burn and undergo free radical substitution with halogens in ultraviolet light. Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes. Alkenes, with general formula C n H 2 n for one double bond, contain a pi bond and undergo electrophilic addition, with the more stable carbocation giving the major product. Potassium manganate seven oxidises alkenes to diols when cold and cleaves them when hot. Alkenes form addition polymers, which are often persistent waste, so reuse, recycling and carefully controlled energy recovery all matter. Now try the mastery check.

Cracking breaks large AL-kaynz into smaller AL-kaynz and AL-keenz. AL-keenz, with general formula C n H 2 n for one double bond, contain a PIE bond and undergo ih-LEK-troh-FIL-ik addition, with the more stable KAR-boh-KAT-eye-un giving the major product. Potassium MANG-uh-nayt seven oxidises AL-keenz to diols when cold and cleaves them when hot. items.prompt: Why are alkanes generally unreactive?

options.text: They contain double bonds that are hard to break
Their C–C and C–H σ bonds are strong with low polarity, and they have no functional group

items.explanation: Strong σ bonds (high activation energies), low polarity and no functional group mean there are no electron-poor or electron-rich sites for attack.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why alkanes are generally unreactive towards nucleophiles?

options.text: Their C–H bonds are only weakly polar, so they lack strongly electron-deficient centres

Their molecules contain a π bond that repels nucleophiles

items.explanation: Carbon and hydrogen differ little in electronegativity, so C–H bonds are only weakly polar and there is no strongly electron-deficient carbon for a nucleophile to attack.

items.prompt: Which pair of features helps to explain why alkanes resist attack by electrophiles?

Weak C–C bonds and lone pairs

items.explanation: Electrophiles attack regions of high electron density. Alkanes have only strong σ bonds, so many reactions have high activation energies.

summary.recapScript: Let us recap the chapter. Open chain alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula C n H 2 n plus 2. They are fairly unreactive because their sigma bonds are strong and of low polarity, they have no functional group, and many reactions have high activation energies, but they burn and undergo free radical substitution with halogens in ultraviolet light. Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes. Alkenes, with general formula C n H 2 n for one double bond, contain a pi bond and undergo electrophilic addition, with the more stable carbocation giving the major product. Potassium manganate seven oxidises alkenes to diols when cold and cleaves them when hot. Alkenes form addition polymers, which are often persistent waste, so reuse, recycling and carefully controlled energy recovery all matter. Now try the mastery check.
takeaways: Alkanes are fairly unreactive (strong, low-polarity bonds, no functional group, high activation energies); they burn and undergo radical substitution.
Alkenes react by electrophilic addition because of the exposed π bond.
Give reagents, conditions, observations and curly arrows in full.

extensionActivity.title: Unplugged and Virtual Practical Set: Hydrocarbons
materials: Molecular model kits, or modelling clay and cocktail sticks (teacher-supplied)
Paper, coloured pencils, string or paper strips for polymer chains
Teacher-supplied photographs or video of the reactions below (virtual demonstrations)
Scenario cards describing local plastic waste (for example sachet water bags or bottles in Ghana)
steps: Activity 1, models: build butane and 2-methylpropane; check both are C₄H₁₀ and decide which boils lower and why. Objective: isomerism and boiling point. Record: formula, shape.
Activity 2, tetrahedral versus planar: build methane and ethene. Measure angles with a protractor. Objective: 109.5° versus 120°. Record: shapes.
Activity 3, rotation: rotate the C–C bond in ethane and try the C=C in ethene. Objective: no rotation about C=C. Record: what you observe.

Activity 4, virtual bromine water test: from a teacher video or photographs, record the colour for hexane and hexene. Expected: orange stays with the alkane; orange becomes colourless with the alkene.

Activity 5, mild versus strong oxidation (teacher demonstration or video only): record the colour of acidified manganate(VII) with an alkene when cold and dilute, and discuss how hot concentrated conditions differ. Expected: purple becomes colourless.
Activity 6, polymer chains: use paper strips as monomers, open the double bond, and join six to make a chain. Draw the repeat unit for ethene, propene and chloroethene.

Activity 7, waste evaluation: for a given plastic waste scenario, compare landfill, reuse, mechanical recycling, chemical recycling and energy recovery, and state one advantage and one hazard of each.

Activity 8, reflection (coursebook p319): work in pairs; one writes a question and mark scheme on free-radical substitution, the other on electrophilic addition, then swap, answer and mark each other’s work.
extensionActivity.safetyNote: Models, video and paper only unless a teacher supervises under school safety rules. Bromine and manganate(VII) are toxic or corrosive; hydrocarbons are flammable. Never burn plastics: the fumes (CO, HCl, dioxins) are hazardous.
extensionActivity.expectedObservation: Branched isomers are more compact and boil lower; C=C is planar with 120° angles and does not rotate; the alkene decolourises bromine water; polymer repeat units contain no C=C; each disposal method has trade-offs.
